guard: no shipped file may import the private, unpublished test-only kit — every src tree in the workspace plus the two entry points of the published cotal-ai package
why: THESE MUTATIONS RUN IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION FROM THE USUAL ONE, on purpose, and a reviewer
should expect that rather than read it as a mistake. The usual shape breaks an implementation and
watches the suite notice. This suite has no implementation under it: its subject is the TREE, and
the property is an absence. Breaking the guard itself can only ever turn a red into a green, which
is a false negative and is not gradable — mutation-proof requires a red to grade. So the mutation
introduces the VIOLATION the guard exists to catch. That is the only direction that proves the
thing worth proving: not that the guard code runs, but that it DETECTS.
TWO SURFACES, TWO MUTATIONS, because they are found by different code. The src trees are
discovered by walking the workspace tiers; the published `cotal-ai` entry points are named
explicitly, because `bin` ships two top-level files and has no `src` tree at all. A single
mutation would have proved one path and left the other asserted. The bin path is also the one
that matters most: it is the exact package a customer installs, and an import of an unpublished
package there is missing at install time rather than at build time here.
THE THIRD MUTATION IS ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT, NOT THE RAIL. A scanner that finds nothing to scan
reports zero offenders and reads as a clean sweep — the same failure as a grep for a string that
no longer exists anywhere: it returns zero and looks healthy while measuring nothing. The suite
refuses that case explicitly, and this mutation is what shows the refusal fires instead of the
reassuring zero.
THE FOURTH GUARDS THE REASON, NOT THE RESULT. The kit stays out of the release train, and it is
tempting to credit `private: true` for that. Measured, that credit is misplaced: a private
example package with no `ignore` entry is versioned anyway, because changesets bumps dependents
and it declares a first-party dependency. What actually keeps the kit out is that it declares no
dependencies at all. That makes zero-dependencies load-bearing, and a load-bearing property with
no assertion under it is a property until the first person adds a convenient import. This
mutation adds one and watches the rail refuse it.
THE FOURTH ALSO NEEDS AN `afterRestore`, AND FINDING OUT WHY IS THE REASON IT IS WRITTEN DOWN.
It mutates a package.json inside a pnpm workspace, and pnpm syncs the lockfile when it runs a
script against a changed manifest. So the first run of this fixture killed all four mutations,
restored all four files, verified the restore, reported success — and left `pnpm-lock.yaml`
carrying `packages/smoke-kit: dependencies: yaml`. The tool restores what it mutated; it cannot
know what the RUN wrote. That is the same shape as a `dist/` compiled from a mutant after the
source is put back, and it is worse here: the lockfile is tracked, so the residue is one
`git commit -a` away from shipping a manifest nobody wrote.
AND THE OBVIOUS REPAIR DOES NOT WORK, WHICH IS WHY THE RESTORE IS A `git checkout`. Regenerating
with `pnpm install --lockfile-only` reports `Already up to date` and leaves the entry in place,
with or without `--force`: pnpm syncs a lockfile ADDITIVELY here and will not prune an importer
entry the manifest no longer declares. Worse, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, which is what CI
runs in seven places, ACCEPTS the residue and exits 0. So nothing downstream would have caught
it: not the regenerate, not the gate that exists to catch exactly this. git is the only thing
that restores it, which is also why this tool refuses to start on a dirty tree. Measured, all
three, rather than reasoned about.
